also: may I hit you for a loan?

evidence: Cic. Att. 7.3.11: ā Caeliō mūtuābimur, we’ll borrow from Caelius
Cic. Att. 15.15.3: cōgor mūtuārī, I am forced to borrow
terms.comment: Of money above all; also of words or ideas taken from another (Quint. 1.5.58: sīcut illī ā nōbīs nōnnumquam mūtuantur, as they sometimes borrow from us).

terms.gloss: ask to borrow, borrow (a thing, to use and give back)
terms.grammar: verb phrase: the gerundive agrees with the thing borrowed
evidence: Plaut. Aul. 400: artoptam ex proximō ūtendam petō
terms.comment: Also ūtendum rogāre (Cato); to lend a thing so is ūtendum dare (Plaut. Asin. 444).

evidence: Caes. BC 1.39.3: ā tribūnīs mīlitum centuriōnibusque mūtuās pecūniās sūmpsit

terms.gloss: hit (someone) for money, touch for a loan
terms.grammar: feriō, fourth conjugation, with the person as object; Traupman adds mūtuō (argentō)
evidence: Ter. Ph. 1.1.13 (Lewis & Short), s.v. feriō: “to cozen, cheat, gull, trick (mostly in vulg. lang.; not in Cic.)”
Traupman 100, 102: ferīre aliquem mūtuō argentō; licet tē mūtuō ferīre?
terms.comment: Comic slang, “to strike” someone for money; it leans to fleecing rather than honest borrowing. The plain way is mūtuārī.

phrases.english: ‘Let’s pay,’ you say. All right, we’ll borrow from Caelius.

phrases.latin: ego hinc artoptam ex proximō ūtendam petō ā Congriōne.
phrases.english: I’ll go and borrow a bread-pan from next door, from Congrio.

phrases.latin: Duās aut trēs familiās habeat, unde ūtenda roget et quibus det, praetereā nēminī.
phrases.english: Let him have two or three households to borrow things from and to lend them to, and no one else.
